questions.prompt: Why does the chapter treat obscurity as a strategic weakness?
choices: Because unseen value often never gets the chance to become influence
Because quiet work is always low quality
Because attention automatically proves merit

explanation.gentle: Yes. The law says that if people do not notice you, they cannot interpret or act around your value.
explanation.direct: Obscurity is costly because recognition is usually a gate condition for leverage.
explanation.competitive: Right. Invisible strength may be real, but it still cannot move the room.

questions.prompt: What does a startling quality do in this chapter's logic?
choices: It guarantees long-term respect immediately
It forces the eye off the background and wins a first look
It removes the need for substance later

explanation.gentle: That is the point. Distinctiveness helps someone rise out of the crowd enough to be noticed.
explanation.direct: A startling quality does not finish the whole job. It interrupts indifference and earns the first moment of attention.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. Contrast gets the room to look up before it drifts on.

questions.prompt: Why does mystery help sustain attention?
choices: Because people keep interpreting what they cannot fully place
Because mystery makes all criticism impossible
Because vague behavior is always respected

explanation.gentle: Yes. The unfinished image stays active because people keep returning to it in thought and conversation.
explanation.direct: Mystery extends attention by keeping interpretation open rather than settled.
explanation.competitive: Correct. An open file keeps getting reopened.

questions.prompt: Talia's presentations are excellent but easy to forget. Which move best fits the chapter?
choices: Keep the presentation exactly the same and trust the room to notice quality eventually
Shock the audience with unrelated theatrics so nobody can ignore her
Add one memorable contrast that wins the room's first look without overwhelming the substance

explanation.gentle: That move fits the law. She needs visibility that serves the work rather than noise that replaces it.
explanation.direct: Option A uses strategic contrast. Option B leaves value trapped in obscurity, and option C risks the wrong spotlight.
explanation.competitive: Right. Win the eyes cleanly, then let the substance cash the look.

questions.prompt: Graham wants to stand out in theater club. What should he avoid?
choices: Choosing one controlled performance detail that makes people look up
Becoming louder than everyone else until he is memorable for disruption
Letting visibility support a credible stage presence

explanation.gentle: That is the trap. The chapter warns that attention can fix the wrong reputation if it comes through bad spectacle.
explanation.direct: He needs attention that supports authority, not noise that brands him unserious.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. Bad spotlight still writes a file, and he may hate what it says.

questions.prompt: Iris keeps overexplaining herself at social gatherings. Which principle is most relevant?
choices: Leave some unresolved space so interest can keep moving toward her
Explain even more so nobody has to wonder about anything
Disappear entirely to create mystery through absence

explanation.gentle: Yes. The chapter treats mystery as controlled unfinishedness, not as total disappearance or exhaustive self-disclosure.
explanation.direct: Option A preserves interpretive motion. Option B exhausts the image, and option C confuses mystery with vanishing.
explanation.competitive: Right. If she empties the whole file at once, there is nothing left to keep the eyes returning.

questions.prompt: What does Mata Hari mainly illustrate in this chapter?
choices: That glamour alone guarantees real power
That layered uncertainty can keep public fascination active
That every famous person is secretly protected from decline

explanation.gentle: That is the chapter's use of her. The fascination stays alive because the image remains unsettled.
explanation.direct: She illustrates mystery as an attention magnifier, not fame as automatic authority.
explanation.competitive: Correct. The public kept staring because the file never fully closed.

questions.prompt: When does attention become strategically harmful under this law?
choices: Whenever more than three people notice you at once
Only when the visible act includes any mystery at all
When it fixes the wrong reputation or provokes the wrong superior

explanation.gentle: That is the limit. Not all attention helps, especially if it makes you memorable in the wrong way.
explanation.direct: Visibility becomes harmful when it supports a bad image or triggers hierarchy backlash.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. A bad spotlight can trap you faster than darkness ever did.

choices: It argues that reputation no longer matters once attention appears
